title: Riftbound is Turing Complete
open: Does there exist a construction of a universal Turing machine in Riftbound that prevents the opponent from interrupting its construction and computation?
status: Stated as open in the source, the paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33839 (2026); no construction is known.
solved_when: An explicit construction is given of a UTM in Riftbound that is protected against any opponent interference, both during the building phase and during the subsequent computation, with a proof of this interruption-resistance.
why: It would show that Riftbound's game mechanics permit not just Turing completeness in principle, but unconditionally reliable computation against adversarial play, closing the gap left by the possibility of opponent interruption.

title: Riftbound is Turing Complete
open: Does there exist a construction of a universal Turing machine in Riftbound in which the actions of all players are forced? That is, can the simulation be arranged so that every player's move is uniquely determined, leaving no genuine choice at any point?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source, the paper arXiv:2609.33839 (2026).
solved_when: An explicit construction of a UTM in Riftbound is given in which all players' actions are forced.
why: It would show that Riftbound's game mechanics alone suffice for deterministic universal computation, ruling out any need for cooperative player choices in the simulation.

title: Riftbound is Turing Complete
open: Does there exist a game-directed strategy in Riftbound for Jayce's Computer under which the Turing machine construction is completed on Jayce's fifth turn or sooner?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.33839 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33839).
solved_when: A strategy is exhibited for Jayce's Computer in Riftbound that is game-directed and completes the Turing machine construction by Jayce's fifth turn or earlier.
why: It pins down how quickly universal computation can be realized within Riftbound, sharpening the paper's Turing-completeness result from mere existence to a concrete turn bound.

title: Riftbound is Turing Complete
open: Is the card game Riftbound computationally universal? The paper leaves as an open exercise the cooperative construction, within Riftbound, of a simulation of an arbitrary Turing machine — ideally by a player and a friend working together.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.33839, which explicitly leaves the construction as an exercise for the reader.
solved_when: An explicit cooperative construction in Riftbound is given that simulates any Turing machine, together with a proof of its correctness.
why: Establishing Turing completeness would place Riftbound among the growing family of games whose mechanics can perform arbitrary computation, with consequences for questions like determining whether a given position is winnable.

title: Quantum Time-Lock Puzzles in the Quantum Random Oracle Model
open: Do quantum-secure time-lock puzzles exist in the quantum random oracle model? That is, can a sender hide a message so that recovering it requires a prescribed amount of sequential computation even against polynomially many parallel quantum processors, with the delay parameter polynomially bounded?
status: The source paper (arXiv 2609.38894) states this problem as open as of 2026, and reports a construction in the quantum random oracle model achieving the above parameters, which it presents as resolving the Mahmoody–Moran–Vadhan question.
solved_when: A construction is given in the quantum random oracle model with generation in one oracle round, solving in at most the prescribed number of oracle rounds, and security against polynomial-width quantum adversaries of depth matching the chosen polynomially bounded delay, for every such delay.
why: It resolves the open problem posed by Mahmoody, Moran, and Vadhan (2011) of building time-lock puzzles that remain secure against quantum adversaries, enabling timed release of information in a post-quantum world.

title: Quantum Time-Lock Puzzles in the Quantum Random Oracle Model
open: Do the impossibility results of Mahmoody, Moran, and Vadhan for time-lock puzzles extend to a setting with quantum honest parties, for instance in the quantum random oracle model?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper, arXiv:2609.38894 (2026); Mahmoody, Moran, and Vadhan left open whether their impossibility result extends to quantum honest parties. No year is given for their work in the record.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that their impossibility result extends to quantum honest parties, in the quantum random oracle model, is established.
why: It would determine whether quantum resources change the fundamental feasibility landscape for time-lock puzzles, a basic primitive for enforcing delayed disclosure of data.

title: Semi-Quantum Cryptography with Certified Deletion
open: Does there exist a semi-quantum cryptographic scheme with certified deletion that can be constructed and proven secure in the plain model, from standard cryptographic assumptions?
solved_when: A plain-model construction of semi-quantum cryptography with certified deletion is given, with a security proof from standard assumptions.
why: It would establish certified deletion without relying on idealized setup, extending deletion guarantees to settings where the classical party has limited quantum capabilities.

title: Verifiable quantum advantage based on polynomials with planted structu
open: Given a cubic Boolean polynomial $g$ and an integer $h$, decide whether $g$ has an independent space of dimension at least $h$.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that correctly decides, for any cubic Boolean polynomial $g$ and integer $h$, whether $g$ has an independent space of dimension at least $h$.
why: Deciding this property would clarify the complexity landscape of the planted-structure polynomial problems underlying this verifiable quantum advantage proposal.

title: Verifiable quantum advantage based on polynomials with planted structu
open: Given a cubic Boolean polynomial $g$ with an independent space $V$ of dimension $h$, find $V$.
solved_when: An algorithm is produced that, given a cubic Boolean polynomial $g$ and the knowledge that it has an independent space $V$ of dimension $h$, outputs $V$.
why: The record gives no motivation beyond extraction from the paper's full text; solving it would advance the planted-structure program for verifiable quantum advantage in the source paper.

title: A physical and universal model of bosonic computations with Solovay-Ki
open: Does the divergent energy observed in the proposed physical model of bosonic computation arise from a heavy-tailed distribution, or from constant probability mass on high occupation numbers? Formally: is the situation that of the fat-tail example, or does the state have constant probability mass on high occupation numbers as in the cited proposition?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source (2026), the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40226.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the source of the energy — either showing it comes from a fat tail as in the example of the paper, or that the state has constant probability mass on high occupation numbers — for the model of https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40226.
why: It determines whether the physical model's infinite energy is a benign tail artifact or a genuine obstruction, which decides whether the model can serve as a universal, physically realizable model of bosonic computation.

title: Computational Bounds for $f$-Routing
open: Can we exhibit an explicit function for which MATH-routing requires superlogarithmic entanglement? More precisely, is there a concrete $f$ whose $f$-routing task provably cannot be accomplished with entanglement growing only logarithmically?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source, arXiv:2609.40278 (2026); no explicit function with superlogarithmic entanglement requirement is known.
solved_when: An explicit function $f$ is given, together with a proof that MATH-routing for that $f$ requires superlogarithmic entanglement.
why: It would supply the first concrete lower-bound instance for entanglement cost in this routing setting, separating logarithmic from superlogarithmic resources.

title: Verifiable Quantum Advantage and Computation via Quantum Circuit Obfus
open: Can general-purpose quantum indistinguishability obfuscation be constructed from standard cryptographic assumptions? That is, can we realize this powerful obfuscation notion for quantum circuits without relying on nonstandard or ill-defined assumptions?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source (2026), in the paper arXiv:2609.40289 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40289).
solved_when: A construction of general-purpose quantum indistinguishability obfuscation is given, together with a proof of security based on standard assumptions.
why: Quantum indistinguishability obfuscation is an extremely strong primitive, and obtaining it from standard assumptions would place verifiable quantum advantage and computation on firm cryptographic footing.

title: Quantum Fine-Grained Lower Bounds for SetDisjointness via Sub-Linear R
open: Does the 3OA problem require $n^{d-o(1)}$ time with the same constant $d$ for all Abelian groups, and can this be established with $d=1$ (or $d=2$ in the classical setting)?
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that, for every Abelian group, 3OA cannot be solved in $n^{d-o(1)}$ time for a constant $d$ that is uniform across all Abelian groups, with $d=1$ in the quantum setting or $d=2$ in the classical setting.
why: It would establish uniform fine-grained hardness for 3OA across all Abelian groups, rather than case-by-case bounds, anchoring quantum and classical time lower bounds for this algebraic problem.

title: Quantum Fine-Grained Lower Bounds for SetDisjointness via Sub-Linear R
open: Can the 3SUM problem be solved in genuinely sublinear quantum time? The conjecture asserts that it cannot: 3SUM admits no $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ quantum-time algorithm for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the conjecture is given: either a quantum lower bound showing 3SUM requires $\Omega(n^{1-o(1)})$ time, or a quantum algorithm running in $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon > 0$.
why: The conjecture underpins quantum fine-grained reductions around set disjointness; establishing it would place quantum 3SUM hardness on firm footing, while a violation would collapse the corresponding lower-bound framework.

title: Quantum Fine-Grained Lower Bounds for SetDisjointness via Sub-Linear R
open: Can the 3SUM problem be solved in $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon > 0$? The conjecture asserts that it cannot: 3SUM admits no classical algorithm running in $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ time for any constant $\varepsilon > 0$.
status: The conjecture is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.40293.
solved_when: An algorithm for 3SUM running in $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon > 0$ is given (refuting the conjecture), or a proof that no such algorithm exists is established (confirming it).
why: The 3SUM conjecture is a cornerstone of fine-grained complexity; resolving it in either direction would settle the true hardness of a wide web of problems reduced to and from 3SUM.

title: Exponential quantum speedup for $\mathbb{F}_3^n$-Subset-Sum? Or, rigor — problem prob:f3-signed-sum
open: Is there a quantum algorithm that finds, in polynomial or at least exponentially-faster-than-classical time, coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m \in \{-1,1\}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m c_i a_i = 0$, given uniformly random vectors $a_1,\dots,a_m \in \mathbb{F}_3^n$? More precisely: does $\mathbb{F}_3^n$-Subset-Sum (the problem prob:f3-signed-sum) admit an exponential quantum speedup, and can such an algorithm be made rigorous?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (2026), arXiv:2609.40321; no algorithm or bound resolving it is given there.
solved_when: A rigorous quantum algorithm is given that, on uniformly random inputs $a_1,\dots,a_m \in \mathbb{F}_3^n$, outputs $c_i \in \{-1,1\}$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^m c_i a_i = 0$, with a provable exponential improvement in running time over the best classical algorithms for this problem.
why: It would exhibit a natural, average-case algebraic problem with a provable exponential quantum advantage, sharpening our understanding of where quantum speedups come from.

title: Blind Unforgeability implies Plus-One Unforgeability
open: Does quantum blind-unforgeability imply quantum plus-one unforgeability? Formally, does any quantum adversary's success in a plus-one forgery experiment bound by the security of the blind-unforgeability notion?
status: Stated as an open question in the source paper arXiv:2610.00517 (2026); no resolution is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation via counterexample) that quantum blind-unforgeability implies quantum plus-one unforgeability is established.
why: Settling the implication clarifies the hierarchy of quantum unforgeability notions for digital signatures and MACs, showing when the stronger blind formulation suffices to guarantee security against the weaker plus-one attack.

title: Approximate Polynomial Satisfiability is in the Counting Hierarchy
open: Can we construct explicit hitting sets for algebraic circuits of a given size? A positive construction would be a major step toward the long-standing goal of explicit hitting sets, a problem intimately connected with algebraic circuit lower bounds.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source paper (arXiv:2610.00644, 2026); no construction is given there.
solved_when: An explicit family of hitting sets is given for the class of polynomials computed by algebraic circuits within the relevant size bounds, matching whatever quantitative parameters the source problem fixes; absent stated parameters, the natural criterion is an explicit hitting set construction for algebraic circuits of the size class in question.
why: Explicit hitting sets are the standard route to derandomizing polynomial identity testing, and their construction is known to be essentially equivalent in difficulty to proving algebraic circuit lower bounds.

title: Exact $T$-counts of CCZ layers from an isotropy bound
open: What are the exact $T$-counts of CCZ layers implied by the isotropy bound? The $T$-count is a dominant cost of fault-tolerant Clifford+$T$ computation, and the bound from isotropy appears not to be tight.
solved_when: The exact $T$-count of the CCZ layers in question is determined, matching or strictly improving the isotropy-based bound.
why: Since $T$-count dominates the cost of fault-tolerant Clifford+$T$ computation, knowing whether the isotropy bound is tight determines whether current CCZ-layer implementations are optimal or leave room for improvement.

title: Exact $T$-counts of CCZ layers from an isotropy bound — openproblem op:gf8
open: What is the exact $T$-count of the $GF(8)$ multiplication oracle? More precisely, determine its precise value, which is known to lie between $20$ and its currently best upper bound.
solved_when: The $T$-count of the $GF(8)$ multiplication oracle is determined exactly, closing the gap between the known lower bound of $20$ and the best known upper bound.
why: An exact count settles whether the isotropy-based lower bound of $20$ is tight for CCZ layers, sharpening the resource estimates for reversible arithmetic in $T$-count-optimized quantum circuits.

title: Cayley HAshing with Matrix Products
open: What is the exact girth of the Cayley graph of the semigroup generated by the matrices $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, taken over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with $p = 2^{256} - 36113$? More precisely, this asks for the length of the shortest nontrivial relation among products of $A$ and $B$ over that ring.
solved_when: The girth of this Cayley graph over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ for $p = 2^{256} - 36113$ is determined exactly.
why: The girth of such Cayley graphs underlies the collision resistance of Cayley hash functions, so an exact value would pin down the security of this concrete parameter choice.

title: Gap Amplification for Local Hamiltonians with Combinatorial Soundness
open: Can the paper's locality-preserving gap amplification results for local Hamiltonians with combinatorial soundness be recovered without the use of friendly postselection? More broadly, given that locality-preserving gap amplification is achieved only with a large alphabet, a natural next step is to study alphabet reduction and proof composition.
solved_when: A construction (or proof) reproduces the paper's locality-preserving gap amplification with combinatorial soundness while eliminating friendly postselection, ideally together with alphabet reduction.
why: Removing friendly postselection would place the gap amplification results on a fully combinatorial footing, and alphabet reduction is the natural prerequisite for proof composition.

title: Optimal and Verifiable Quantum Advantages in Communication Complexity
open: Does a quantum advantage in communication complexity exist that can be achieved with a single quantum message? More precisely, can the advantage attested in the source be realized without additional rounds of interaction?
status: Stated as open in the source, arXiv:2610.05585 (2026).
solved_when: A communication-complexity problem is exhibited for which a single quantum message yields a provable advantage over the corresponding classical setting (or such an advantage is shown impossible).
why: It would pin down whether interaction is essential to the demonstrated quantum advantage, clarifying the minimal communication structure needed for verifiable quantum speedups.

title: The Complexity of Computing Nash Equilibria in Colonel Blotto Games
open: Can a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium be computed efficiently in discrete Colonel Blotto games whose battlefield payoffs are monotonic and piecewise constant? In formal terms, is there a polynomial-time algorithm for this setting, or does the problem admit a hardness result?
status: Stated as an open question (Question 1) by Kontogiannis et al., highlighted in the source paper (arXiv:2610.05956, 2026), which answers it in the negative with hardness results.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that computing Nash equilibria in discrete Colonel Blotto games with monotonic, piecewise constant battlefield payoffs is computationally hard — the source paper answers this question in the negative via hardness results.
why: It settles the basic computational tractability of equilibrium computation in a classic allocation game, delineating which Colonel Blotto variants admit efficient solution methods and which do not.

title: The Complexity of Computing Nash Equilibria in Colonel Blotto Games
open: Does computing Nash equilibria in Colonel Blotto games remain computationally hard when the number of players is a constant? Formally, the question asks whether the hardness shown in the player-specific equal-splitting setting persists when the player count no longer grows with the instance.
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05956. Concurrent work by Bichler and Ghosh established hardness in the same player-specific equal-splitting setting when the number of players grows with the instance, and asked whether hardness persists for a constant number of players.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that computing Nash equilibria in the player-specific equal-splitting Colonel Blotto setting is hard — or polynomial-time computable — when the number of players is constant.
why: It settles a question posed by Bichler and Ghosh in concurrent work, and determines whether hardness of equilibrium computation in Colonel Blotto games is an artifact of a growing number of players or a robust feature of the game itself.

title: Unitary RQL Equals RQL
open: Does unitary randomized query complexity coincide with general randomized query complexity for one-sided bounded-error algorithms? Fefferman and Remscrim explicitly isolated this as Open Problem 1.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that unitary RQL equals RQL in the one-sided bounded-error setting is established.
why: It would settle the last remaining gap between unitary and general randomized query models, clarifying whether coherent, reversible query algorithms are as powerful as arbitrary randomized ones.

title: Explicit Nonlinear Functions beyond the Fourier bound — question ques:min-ind-sets
open: Which $r$-uniform hypergraphs on $n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges have the fewest independent sets? A sharp extremal characterization would settle the question of how small the number of independent sets can be forced to be under these constraints.
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper (arXiv:2610.06362); no progress beyond the posing of the problem is recorded in the census.
solved_when: A complete characterization (or sharp bound) of the $r$-uniform hypergraphs on $n$ vertices with at most $m$ edges that minimize the number of independent sets is given, for the general parameters $r$, $n$, and $m$.
why: It resolves the natural extremal question about independent-set counts in uniform hypergraphs, which underlies questions about explicit nonlinear functions beyond the Fourier bound raised in the source paper.

title: Separating ClonableQMA and QCMA Relative to a Classical Oracle
open: Is there a classical oracle relative to which ClonableQMA and QCMA become provably different complexity classes? That is, does there exist a classical oracle $O$ such that ClonableQMA$^O \neq$ QCMA$^O$?
status: Stated as open (conjecture 5) in the paper 2610.06740 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06740), dated 2026; no separation is known.
solved_when: A classical oracle $O$ is exhibited, together with a proof that ClonableQMA$^O$ and QCMA$^O$ are separated relative to it.
why: Such a separation would clarify whether the ability to clone quantum witnesses genuinely adds power beyond classical witnesses, delineating the boundary between quantum and classical proof systems in the oracle setting.

title: Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Spars
open: Can triangle finding in sparse graphs be used to obtain a truly subquadratic algorithm for 3SUM and a truly subcubic algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths? In other words, is there a reduction through which faster triangle detection in sparse graphs yields algorithms running in o(n²) time for 3SUM and o(n³) time for APSP?
status: The problem is stated as open in the source (2026). Key work: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06783
solved_when: An algorithm (or reduction chain) is exhibited that solves 3SUM in truly subquadratic time and APSP in truly subcubic time — i.e., strictly faster than n² and n³ respectively — via triangle detection in sparse graphs, with the running-time bounds proved.
why: The 3SUM and APSP problems are central hardness benchmarks for fine-grained complexity: a truly subquadratic 3SUM or truly subcubic APSP algorithm would overturn widely used hardness assumptions and unlock faster algorithms for the many problems reduced from them.

title: Characterizing Quantum Advantage for Generalizations of the Boolean Hi
open: Is the quantum–classical separation for problems in the MATH family fully characterized by sign degree rather than pure high degree — that is, do the lower bounds extend from high degree to sign degree of MATH, as conjectured?
solved_when: The previously stated lower bounds are proven to hold for the sign degree of MATH instead of the pure high degree, establishing sign degree as the parameter governing both quantum and classical one-way communication complexities of all problems in the MATH family.
why: It pins down the exact complexity parameter controlling quantum advantage for this family, settling whether the known separations are tight.

title: Private online learning and prediction for Littlestone classes
open: Does every class of finite Littlestone dimension admit a private online learner? A full formal statement would specify the privacy and regret guarantees required, but the source leaves the question at this level of generality.
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), arXiv:2610.06822.
solved_when: A construction or impossibility result is established for private online learning of arbitrary finite-Littlestone-dimension classes, as posed in the source paper (arXiv:2610.06822).
why: It would determine whether the combinatorial structure governing online learnability (Littlestone dimension) also suffices for learnability under privacy constraints in the online setting.

title: An Analysis of Decision Problems for Relational Pattern Languages unde
open: Is the central decision problem for erasing pattern languages decidable in general? This long-standing question — the most significant open problem in decision problems for erasing patterns — remains unresolved.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source (arXiv:2610.07119, 2026), where it is described as the most significant open problem in the field of decision problems for patterns.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of general decidability for the decision problem at issue for erasing pattern languages is given.
why: It is the main obstacle to a complete understanding of decision problems for erasing patterns; settling it would resolve the field's flagship open question.

title: On the Complexity of Mixed Equilibria in First-Price Auctions with Cor
open: What is the computational complexity of deciding whether a mixed Bayes–Nash equilibrium exists in a first-price auction with correlated (correlated-type) bidder distributions? The source paper established NP-hardness for pure BNE in this setting but left the mixed case open.
solved_when: The complexity of deciding the existence of a mixed BNE in first-price auctions with correlated types is resolved — e.g., by a proof of hardness or a polynomial-time decision algorithm.
why: It completes the complexity picture for equilibrium computation in first-price auctions: the pure case is known hard, and the mixed case is the missing half needed to characterize when equilibria can be found or certified efficiently.

title: Associativity of Multiplication Is Hard for Resolution
open: Does the multiplier associativity formula require exponentially large resolution refutations?
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), from paper 2610.08988 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08988); the record indicates the paper resolves this problem by proving an exponential lower bound on the size of resolution refutations of the multiplier associativity formula.
solved_when: A proof of an exponential lower bound on the size of resolution refutations of the multiplier associativity formula is given.
why: It resolves an open problem posed by Beame and Liew and extends our understanding of resolution proof complexity to the associativity of multiplication.

title: Associativity of Multiplication Is Hard for Resolution
open: Is the bit-level tautology expressing associativity of multiplication — that (a·b)·c equals a·(b·c) — hard to refute for stronger proof systems as well? We conjecture that multiplier associativity remains hard for these systems too.
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), arXiv:2610.08988 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08988).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that bit-level multiplier associativity is hard for the proof systems in question; if conditional, hardness must be established for the specific systems the source identifies as extending the known cases.
why: Associativity of multiplication is a natural, simply stated family of tautologies; proving its hardness for stronger systems would separate those systems from Resolution on a concrete arithmetic principle.

title: Separating comb inequalities is NP-hard
open: What is the computational complexity of separating comb inequalities — is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a candidate point, finds a violated comb inequality or certifies none exists? More precisely, determine whether comb separation is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard.
status: Stated as an open question in 2026 in the source paper (arXiv:2610.09065, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09065).
solved_when: A proof that comb separation is NP-hard, or a polynomial-time separation algorithm for comb inequalities, is established.
why: It resolves a longstanding open question in polyhedral combinatorics, closing a basic gap in our understanding of one of the central inequality families for the TSP polytope.

title: The Weakest Assumptions a Protocol Needs
open: Does the extension result hold for the full goal language, in which hypotheses may also contain role-position and parameter atoms, and not just the restricted fragment considered so far?
status: The question is stated as open in the source paper, arXiv:2610.09730 (2026); no progress beyond the statement is recorded.
solved_when: The open question is resolved by a proof (or refutation) that the result extends to the full goal language of the framework of arXiv:2610.09730, where hypotheses may contain role-position and parameter atoms.
why: It would establish the weakest assumptions the protocol framework actually needs, closing the gap between the fragment currently analyzed and the full language in which protocols are naturally written.

title: Polynomial Kernels for Interval Completion
open: Do the Interval Edge Deletion and Interval Edge Editing problems admit polynomial kernels? The authors settle this positively for Interval Completion, but leave the deletion and editing variants open.
status: The source paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10319, stated as open in 2026) provides polynomial kernels for Interval Completion, but leaves open whether polynomial kernels exist for Interval Edge Deletion and Interval Edge Editing.
solved_when: A polynomial-size kernel is established (or ruled out) for Interval Edge Deletion and for Interval Edge Editing.
why: Polynomial kernels are what make parameterized preprocessing practical; extending them from completion to the deletion and editing variants would complete the kernelization picture for interval graphs.

title: The rank of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is 2
open: What is the exact rank of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$? The rank of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and its border rank over $\mathbb{F}_2$ remain open.
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11823.
solved_when: The exact rank (and border rank) of $3\times 3$ matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$ is determined.
why: Determining it would pin down the true arithmetic complexity of small-matrix multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

title: Improved Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing and Worst-C — question q:OPI
open: For a fixed rate $R = k/n$ and fixed $ (0,1)$, what is the largest $s^* (0,1]$ so that every OPI instance of rate $R$ with $|S_i| p$ for all $i$ admits a solution $Q _p[X]$ with satisfaction ratio $s(Q) s^*$? What is the largest fraction $s^*_{ {alg}} (0,1]$ so that a solution $Q _p[X]$ with $s(Q) s^*_{ {alg}}$ can be found efficiently with a quantum algorithm?
status: stated as open in source (2026)

title: Improved Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing and Worst-C — question q:llr
open: What is the smallest rate $R^*$ such that, for every rate $R > R^*$, Shamir's secret-sharing scheme over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $k/n = R$ is one-bit local leakage resilient?
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), the paper arXiv:2610.12357; no bound on $R^*$ is given in the record.
solved_when: An explicit value of $R^*$ is determined (with proof) such that for all $R > R^*$, Shamir over $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $k/n = R$ is one-bit LLR.
why: It pins down the exact rate threshold at which Shamir sharing becomes locally leakage resilient, delineating which instantiations of the most widely used secret-sharing scheme are safe against leakage attacks.
